title: Developers (Anti-Money Laundering and Terrorism Financing) Bill
what_it_is: Developers (Anti-Money Laundering and Terrorism Financing) Bill

sections.label: Real estate money laundering amendments
sections.summary: The Bill amends both Acts to require developers to detect money laundering and terrorism financing and to bar convicted persons from developer activities.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: Real estate is a category of the non-financial sector that may encounter persons engaging in money laundering and terrorism financing activities.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: So, this Bill amends both Acts to, firstly, put in place new requirements for developers to facilitate the detection of money laundering and terrorism financing and, secondly, bar persons from being involved in developer activities if they have been convicted for money laundering and terrorism financing offences.

sections.label: Developer due diligence duties
sections.summary: Developers must carry out customer due diligence checks on purchasers, keep proper records, and report suspicious transactions to Suspicious Transaction Reporting Officers.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: In particular, developers will need to carry out customer due diligence checks on purchasers, keep proper records relating to these checks, and report any suspicious transactions to the Suspicious Transaction Reporting Officers (STROs).

sections.label: Penalty for non-compliance
sections.summary: The penalty for not complying with these provisions is a fine not exceeding $100,000.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: The penalty for not complying with the above provisions will be a fine not exceeding $100,000.

sections.label: Consultation and compliance burden balance
sections.summary: Non-compliance risks international business relationships and reputation; after consulting REDAS, the Law Society and the public, the Bill seeks to balance regulatory burden with international standards and FATF Recommendations.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: Failure of businesses to meet international standards puts at risk our international business relationships, as well as the reputation of individual companies and the Singapore financial market in general.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: We have consulted the Real Estate Developers Association (REDAS), the Law Society of Singapore and members of the public in general.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: They appreciate the reputational risks of non-compliance with international standards and are supportive of the proposed anti-money laundering and terrorism financing requirements.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: The industry has shared concerns on the additional compliance burden that may be generated and how they can effectively carry out their new duties.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: We understand these concerns and, in drafting the Bill, we have sought to strike a balance between the additional regulatory burden imposed on the industry as well as the need to meet international standards and the FATF Recommendations.

sections.label: Serious crimes penalties Bill passed
sections.summary: Parliament passed the Serious Crimes and Counter-Terrorism (Miscellaneous Amendments) Bill yesterday for tougher penalties on corporations, professional service providers and money mules.

sentences.speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
sentences.text: Parliament had passed the Serious Crimes and Counter-Terrorism (Miscellaneous Amendments) Bill yesterday to provide for tougher penalties on corporations and professional service providers, as well as money mules for overseas organised syndicates.

sections.label: Developer requirements in proposed Bill
sections.summary: The proposed Bill requires developers to carry out customer due diligence, keep proper records and report suspicious transactions.

sentences.speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
sentences.text: The proposed Bill puts in place requirements for developers to carry out customer due diligence, keep proper records and report suspicious transactions.

sections.label: Overseas shell companies owning UK properties
sections.summary: A Financial Times article says about 100,000 properties in England and Wales are owned by overseas companies, many bought by anonymous offshore shell companies.

sentences.speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
sentences.text: According to an article by the Financial Times on "How laundered money shapes London's property market", about 100,000 properties in England and Wales are owned by overseas companies, with many of the properties having been bought by anonymous shell companies based in offshore tax havens.

sections.label: Protecting genuine buyers from compliance costs
sections.summary: The speaker asks that genuine buyers of Singapore homes be protected from increased compliance costs developers may pass on under the Bill.

sentences.speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
sentences.text: My final point is to ask, once again, that genuine buyers of Singapore homes be protected from any increased cost of compliance by developers, which the introduction of this Bill may inadvertently cause.

sentences.speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
sentences.text: We can do that by adopting a calibrated risk-based approach.

sections.label: Developer due diligence and compliance consistency
sections.summary: The Bill requires developers to perform customer due diligence, keep records and report suspicious transactions, and the speaker asks how consistency and compliance will be ensured.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: The Bill requires developers to perform customer due diligence (CDD), maintain records and report on suspicious transactions, amongst other measures.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: How will the Ministry ensure consistency in the way different developers perform such checks and how can it ensure compliance from all developers so that these measures will not end up as a matter of formality?

sections.label: Preventing money laundering through this avenue
sections.summary: The speaker asks how the Ministry will prevent money laundering through this avenue.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: How will the Ministry prevent money laundering through this avenue?

sections.label: REDAS feedback on verifying purchaser profiles
sections.summary: REDAS feedback states there are practical limitations on how developers can conclusively check or verify a purchaser's profile and transactional patterns during a sale and purchase transaction.

sentences.speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: According to feedback from the Real Estate Developers' Association of Singapore (REDAS), there are practical limitations on how developers can conclusively check or verify a purchaser's profile and transactional patterns during a sale and purchase transaction.

sections.label: Revising 12-month CDD timeframe for developers
sections.summary: The speaker asks the Minister to revise the 12-month timeframe for CDD on existing customers and allow developers flexibility, given their lower ML/FT risks.

sentences.speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: The new regulations stipulate a timeframe of 12 months to allow developers to perform CDD measures on its existing customers based on its own assessment of materiality and risk and other considerations.

sentences.speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Considering that the ML/FT risks faced by a developer is lower, as explained earlier, the Minister should consider revising the 12-month timeframe and allow developers some flexibility.

sections.label: Regulation of completed project sales
sections.summary: The speaker asks why the COH regulates only uncompleted project sales and not completed project sales.

sentences.speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: This would not only deprive the development of a legitimate sale but may also incur unhappiness from customers and even lawsuits.

sentences.speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: I note that the COH only regulates the sale of uncompleted projects.

sentences.speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: What is the reason that sale of completed projects is not required to be regulated?

sections.label: Developer checks on suspicious buyers
sections.summary: The Bill requires developers to check whether a client has a suspicious background and bars selling to such a buyer.

sentences.speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: According to the Bill, the developers must check whether the client has a suspicious background and, if found to be so, they cannot sell the property to this buyer.

sections.label: Government stance on unexplained wealth order
sections.summary: The speaker asks the Government's stance on the unexplained wealth order and whether it will consider implementing it.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: What is the Government’s stance on the unexplained wealth order and will the Government consider implementing it in the law?

sections.label: Unexplained wealth order for AML/CFT
sections.summary: The speaker cites Transparency International on London properties and asks if the Ministry would adopt unexplained wealth legislation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Transparency International has identified £4.4 billion worth of London properties that it says were paid for by illicit funds and argues that an unexplained wealth order is a crucial tool for governments to combat the use of such dirty money.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: An unexplained wealth order would complement this law by tackling the demand side of the problem.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Would the Ministry consider adopting unexplained wealth legislation to bolster our AML/CFT regime?

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: This Bill goes some way towards achieving that.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: But let us clarify what it means for local businesses and see how much more we can do.

sections.label: AML/CFT rules for estate agents
sections.summary: CEA has due diligence guidelines for estate agents, and amendments to the Estate Agents Act are intended next year.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: For real estate agents, in particular, the Council for Estate Agencies (CEA) already has guidelines to require estate agents to perform due diligence checks for suspicious transactions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: However, we do intend to make amendments next year to the Estate Agents Act so as to impose similar AML/CFT requirements for estate agents.

sections.label: Due diligence deadline in subsidiary legislation
sections.summary: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah raised the 12-month due diligence deadline, which will be set out in undecided subsidiary legislation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah, for example, talked about the 12-month deadline when due diligence checks are to be conducted.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: These are more detailed regulations that would be set out in subsidiary legislation and we have not decided on them yet.

sections.label: Prescribed period after transaction
sections.summary: The prescribed period will be in the rules and is at least five years after the transaction is completed.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: The prescribed period will be set out in the rules and will be at least five years after the completion of the transaction.

sections.label: Developer CDD measures required
sections.summary: Under new statutory provisions, a developer must perform prescribed CDD measures at prescribed times.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Under the new section 12B of the Housing Developers (Control and Licensing) Act and the new section 5A(2) of the Sale of Commercial Properties Act, a developer is required to perform such CDD measures as may be prescribed, at such times as may be prescribed.

sections.label: Developer and officer liability
sections.summary: The developer is primarily responsible for failing due diligence, but officers may also be liable for consent, connivance or negligence.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Indeed, the developer will be primarily responsible for failing to perform any due diligence measures as required by law.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: However, where the offence was committed with the consent or connivance of an officer of the company, or the commission of the offence was attributable to the officer's negligence, then that officer may also be held liable for the offence.

sections.label: URA audits and penalties
sections.summary: URA's COH will audit developers, and non-compliance may bring fines or disqualification from future licences.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Then, when the industry's capabilities are levelled up, when everything is in motion, the COH under URA will carry out regular audit checks to ensure that, indeed, developers are implementing their measures properly.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: And if developers are found to not have adhered to the requirements, there will be penalties, not only potential fines, but, in more serious cases, they could also be disqualified from obtaining licences in the future.

sections.label: Jurisdictions committed to FATF
sections.summary: About 190 jurisdictions have committed to the FATF Recommendations to date.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: To date, about 190 jurisdictions have committed to the FATF Recommendations.

sections.label: Overseas convictions and licences
sections.summary: Local convictions mainly ground licence refusal, suspension or revocation, but overseas convictions may also be considered with other circumstances.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh also asked if we can deny or revoke a housing developer's licence to persons or entities that have been convicted of ML/TF offences in other jurisdictions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: We will mainly rely on local convictions as a basis to refuse, suspend or revoke a Housing Developer's Licence.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: But the Controller may refuse to grant a Licence to a person or entity with an overseas conviction, or revoke the licence if it has been earlier granted, if the overseas conviction, together with other circumstances, indicates that it is carrying on its business in Singapore in a manner that is detrimental to the interests of purchasers or to the public.
